text: Lesson 9 covered pulling every alert and event tied to an incident's entities into one working set. Timeline reconstruction is the next step: putting that set in chronological order across every system that logged a piece of it. No single log tells the whole story - each system only sees its own slice of what happened.

Say an investigation pulls events from four systems tied to one compromised account and host. Email security logged a phishing message at 8:47am. Identity logs show a sign-in with harvested credentials at 9:02am - initial access. Endpoint logs show a remote session to a file server at 9:15am - lateral movement. The file server then shows an archive created in a temp folder at 9:40am - data staging.

None of those four entries, read alone inside its own system's log, looks like an attack in progress. A sign-in is routine. A remote session is routine. An archive file is routine. Lined up by timestamp across all four sources, after normalizing to one time zone, they stop looking routine and read as exactly what they are: a full attack chain from phishing email to staged data in under an hour.

Building the timeline means collecting the relevant events from each source, normalizing timestamps to one time zone - logs from different systems often record in different zones or formats, and a timeline built on mismatched clocks puts events in the wrong order and can hide which event actually came first - then sorting the full set chronologically into one sequence an analyst can read top to bottom, the same way Sentinel's entity timeline shows one entity's history.

Order is what turns a list of facts into a timeline. Knowing data staging followed lateral movement by 25 minutes, which followed initial access by 13 minutes, is the finding that drives the next question: what else did the attacker touch in that window. That's Lesson 11's scoping question, and it leads straight into Chapter 4's containment decisions.
